title: Heathrow expansion: a cheaper, phased alternative and the trade-offs
label: 14 October 2026 · Heathrow expansion scrutiny
summary: Members of the Transport Committee questioned Heathrow West Ltd (HWL) about its alternative proposal for Heathrow expansion: a smaller, phased runway plan they say is cheaper, quicker and less environmentally damaging than Heathrow Airport Ltd’s scheme. HWL stressed affordability, airline support and deliverability; ministers, regulators and local communities would still need to judge noise, biodiversity, air quality, surface access and carbon impacts. The witnesses argued the National Policy Statement needs clearer weighting of tests and said many environmental and infrastructure risks affect viability.

glossary.definition: Heathrow Expansion National Policy Statement, the Government’s planning policy for the proposed new runway.
National Policy Statement, a Government document that sets planning policy for major infrastructure.
Development Consent Order, the legal permission developers need to build nationally significant projects.
Department for Transport, the UK government department responsible for transport policy.
Civil Aviation Authority, the UK regulator for aviation including promoting competition and safety.
Sustainable aviation fuel, lower-carbon fuel made from sustainable sources to reduce plane emissions.
Getting people to change from private cars to public transport, walking or cycling for journeys to the airport.
UK government target for the country’s emissions to be balanced by removals by 2050.
Take-offs and landings; often shortened to 'movements' when describing airport capacity.

chapters.title: Why HWL says Heathrow must expand – and how their plan differs
chapters.takeaway: Heathrow West argues expansion is essential for UK connectivity and proposes a smaller, phased runway to reduce cost, speed delivery and lower environmental impact.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: We’re looking at the Government’s draft Heathrow expansion policy. Could you explain why expansion matters and whether the NPS makes that case?

turns.speaker: Surinder Arora
turns.text: Heathrow’s expansion has been discussed for decades. We need the connectivity for business and jobs or other hubs — Dubai, Schiphol — will take that role. The NPS recognises the need, but specifics matter.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: You’ve been developing an alternative runway plan. Was that under way before the Government’s announcements?

turns.speaker: Surinder Arora
turns.text: Yes. We’ve worked on expansion ideas for over ten years and fed our analysis into the NPS process.

turns.speaker: Carlton Brown
turns.text: Our scheme focuses on affordable growth, employment and national benefits. We think the assessment should be clearer about how different economic benefits are weighted against each other.

turns.speaker: Jacob Collier
turns.text: What are the main advantages of your proposal versus HAL’s?

turns.speaker: Surinder Arora
turns.text: We listened to airlines: they want affordability and deliverability. Our plan phases construction, is cheaper, uses less land and can open faster — so jobs and connectivity come sooner.

turns.speaker: Carlton Brown
turns.text: Smaller scheme means less environmental impact, lower cost and quicker delivery, so the economy benefits sooner than with a much larger, more expensive build.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: You say your business case stacks up. But will regulators and the Secretary of State accept your plan?

turns.speaker: Surinder Arora
turns.text: That’s for PINS, the Secretary of State and the regulators to decide. We’ve spent millions preparing a business case and believe it is deliverable.

chapters.title: Design, phasing and operational questions
chapters.takeaway: HWL proposes a 2.4 km runway in phase 1 (extendable later); they argue it meets many airline needs but raises practical questions about construction, aircraft types and future resilience.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Your scheme phases a 2.4 km runway, later extendable. Can you keep the runway open while you extend it safely?

turns.speaker: Surinder Arora
turns.text: We’ve discussed this with airlines and constructors. It can be done; practical design work, including precast risers and limits on plant, makes phased construction workable.

turns.speaker: Carlton Brown
turns.text: Bechtel and Stantec have studied the construction. We’d pre-build the safety riser so subsequent works don’t block operations. There are constraints, but they’re manageable.

turns.speaker: Dr Arthur
turns.text: Passengers from regions want direct long-haul flights. If your phased runway limits wide-body operations, doesn’t that reduce direct connections?

turns.speaker: Surinder Arora
turns.text: We can handle some wide-body aircraft depending on load, temperature and wind. Airlines told us 2.4–2.8 km can meet many operational needs and keep regional connectivity.

turns.speaker: Jacob Collier
turns.text: What are your biggest risks to affordability and deliverability?

turns.speaker: Carlton Brown
turns.text: Key risks are climate-related requirements, surface access costs, community compensation and whether phase 2 becomes commercially viable; affordability should be a pass/fail test.

turns.speaker: Scott Witchalls
turns.text: We designed a smaller footprint to create more ‘headroom’ in the business case — less land take and lower construction carbon reduce some risk, but detailed modelling is ongoing.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: HAL’s numbers vary in public debate — you’ve said the total expansion figures are large. Does competition matter?

turns.speaker: Carlton Brown
turns.text: We believe the expansion package — widely quoted at very high sums — should face competition. The CAA’s duty includes promoting competition, and the NPS shouldn’t lock out other promoters.

chapters.title: Climate, air quality and surface access
chapters.takeaway: HWL accepts it cannot deliver wider decarbonisation alone; it proposes measures on construction, energy and rail-ready design but worries that uncertain future costs (SAF, removals) threaten viability.

turns.speaker: Chris Hinchliff
turns.text: DfT assumes displacement from other airports for 74% of Heathrow’s extra passengers. Is that realistic and does it affect carbon and viability?

turns.speaker: Carlton Brown
turns.text: Airlines decide routes; Heathrow is the UK’s hub and needs feeder traffic. The displacement assumption is complex but airlines will shape the outcome.

turns.speaker: Chris Hinchliff
turns.text: The Climate Change Committee says the industry should cover 100% of environmental costs and have contingency measures. Would that risk your scheme's viability?

turns.speaker: Carlton Brown
turns.text: It could. Extra requirements increase costs and may jeopardise viability. That’s why we argue affordability must be a formal pass or fail test alongside the four statutory tests.

turns.speaker: Scott Witchalls
turns.text: Our scheme reduces construction and whole-life carbon by being smaller. But decarbonising flying itself depends on SAF, new tech and removals, which promoters cannot deliver alone.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: You’ve proposed rail-ready works and a rail box under a new terminal. Do you depend on the western and southern rail links to meet modal shift targets?

turns.speaker: Carlton Brown
turns.text: We don’t rely on those links opening by 2035. We’ll design to connect to them, use construction rail where possible, and push bus, coach and other measures to increase public transport use over time.

turns.speaker: Daniel Francis
turns.text: Who should pay for airport-related rail: the airport operator or wider taxpayers?

turns.speaker: Carlton Brown
turns.text: Users should pay their share, but if rail helps wider communities, the split needs regulator and DfT oversight. The detail must be agreed with the CAA and Government.

turns.speaker: Scott Witchalls
turns.text: On power and airside electrification, we plan an energy centre, heat pumps and on-site charging to reduce reliance on an overloaded grid for apron electrification.

turns.speaker: Alex Mayer
turns.text: Have you modelled climate impacts like heavier rainfall or higher temperatures on runway performance?

turns.speaker: Scott Witchalls
turns.text: Yes — design uses a one-in-100-year plus climate change standard for drainage and runway performance; detailed modelling is part of the design work.

turns.speaker: Steff Aquarone
turns.text: Air quality tests in the NPS are legal thresholds, but do they force improvements? Could expansion erase recent air quality gains?

turns.speaker: Carlton Brown
turns.text: Surface access is the main air quality lever. We will model EV uptake, bus and coach improvements and other measures, but setting how strict targets should be is for policy makers and local people.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: What about aircraft-related ultra-fine particles (UFPs)? Should they be monitored and regulated?

turns.speaker: Scott Witchalls
turns.text: UFPs should be monitored; standards are evolving. We’ll work to current NPS requirements and adapt if standards change.

chapters.title: Communities, noise and biodiversity
chapters.takeaway: HWL says it will meet or exceed the mitigation promised under HAL’s plans, but biodiversity loss, noise displacement and compensation are significant concerns best tested at the DCO stage.

turns.speaker: Dr Arthur
turns.text: Would regional passengers lose direct services if Heathrow concentrates long-haul there?

turns.speaker: Surinder Arora
turns.text: Some regional direct routes exist and we want more. But long-haul often needs the hub scale that only Heathrow can provide — you can’t replicate that with smaller regional airports.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Your runway starts a bit further east than HAL’s. Would that change who gets noise and insulation?

turns.speaker: Carlton Brown
turns.text: Our runway is 195 metres east; noise modelling shows the difference in contours is very small — less than human hearing threshold in many cases — but communities will be affected and must be consulted.

turns.speaker: Steff Aquarone
turns.text: Is your community compensation based on HAL’s 2018 proposals, and should compensation be set in the NPS or left to DCO?

turns.speaker: Surinder Arora
turns.text: We’ll at least match the current commitments and hope to do better. The NPS can set minimums, but detailed compensation and delivery are examined and refined at DCO stage.

turns.speaker: Chris Hinchliff
turns.text: The sustainability appraisal says major adverse biodiversity effects are likely even with mitigation. Does promoting this scheme concern you amid a nature crisis?

turns.speaker: Carlton Brown
turns.text: A third runway will cause harm. Our smaller footprint reduces it versus a larger runway. We’re planning ecological enhancements and biodiversity offsetting, but some loss is unavoidable.

turns.speaker: Chris Hinchliff
turns.text: If biodiversity measures fail over time, who would be responsible to fix them?

turns.speaker: Carlton Brown
turns.text: That’s why the DCO examination must test delivery, management and long-term stewardship. Responsibility and monitoring arrangements should be defined before consent is granted.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: In short, your team says your plan is cheaper, quicker and less impactful, but many environmental, surface access and commercial risks remain — and Government, regulators and PINS must test them in detail?

turns.speaker: Surinder Arora
turns.text: Exactly. We believe our plan gives the UK better value and quicker benefits, but these are complex trade-offs and the democratic and regulatory process must judge which scheme best meets national needs.
